sentences.text: Bori's understanding of the arrangement, at twelve, came mostly from her grandmother, who had put one out every year since 1961 and who talked about it the way other people talk about the gas bill.
The most important thing — the thing that took Bori longest to accept, and that she got wrong at first the way everybody gets it wrong at first — was that the letters are not delivered.
Nobody receives one.
Ever.
There is no story in Szentmárton about a woman in Debrecen who found a piece of paper in her yard, and no story about anybody learning anything they did not know.
Bori went looking for such a story on purpose, at seven, asking seven adults, and got nine blank looks and one raised eyebrow.
They are taken away.
Bori's first version of the arrangement, at about eight, had been the obvious one: that the geese were postmen, and that somewhere there were people opening things.
She had liked that version.
It had a shape.

She had built quite a lot on it before her grandmother took it apart in about four sentences one afternoon, and she remembers being genuinely upset, and she remembers her grandmother being entirely unsympathetic about the upset.
That is what the geese do.

They come over low on one night in October and they take the year's unsaid things out of the village, and where they go with them is not anybody's business, and Bori's grandmother had views about people who asked.
"But then what's the point?" Her grandmother was mending something and did not look up.
"Say it out loud, then.
Say the thing to the person.
Go on." Bori said that was not fair.
"It isn't fair.
I know exactly what's in mine and I've known for sixty-four years and I'd sooner have my hand in the fire than say it in this kitchen." She bit the thread.
"But I can put it down.

Once a year I can put it down and it goes somewhere and it is not in this house any more, and in the morning I can look at your grandfather across that table." Bori did not have anything to say to that.
"It isn't a solution, kislány.
It's a place to put a thing.
There aren't many, and they're worth knowing about." Bori asked her, once, and only once, whether it was the same thing every year.
Her grandmother put the mending down, which she did not do, and looked at the window for a while.
"For about thirteen years it was," she said.
"Then it stopped being, and then for a long time it was small things, and now for the last few years it's been the same one again, but it's not the same one it was at the start.
It's the other end of it." That was the entire conversation and Bori has thought about it for twenty years.
There was one more rule, which was not a rule so much as a fact everybody had learned by observation.
Once it is out, it is out.
You do not go and get it back.
Not because anything happens to you if you do.
Nothing happens to you.

Bori's uncle had gone out and retrieved his in 2009 at about half past ten, having thought better of it, and had come in with the paper in his hand and had been perfectly fine and had burnt it in the stove.
But he had not put one out since, and he was not the same at that kitchen table, and Bori's grandmother had said one sentence about it in fifteen years, which was: *he's still carrying it.*
